summary:
The Republic of Mordovia stands under the national framework of Russia, which applies in full; the assessment is made at the national level, with no regional deviation identified for Mordovia.

Russia presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes to official documents was signed; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression that, explicitly, includes anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, detention of up to 15 days, and deportation, and national government warnings directed at LGBT travellers say so plainly.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Russia (June 2025) records that same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, while same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, gender-marker changes on official documents are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023. The 2013 "gay propaganda" statute is punishable by administrative fines or detention of up to 15 days, escalating to up to four years' imprisonment on a repeat offence. Since the 2023 extremist designation of the international LGBT+ movement, participation carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising carries six to ten years.

The same note records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024, and assesses that openly LGBT+ people face societal discrimination that may amount to persecution, with the state able but unwilling to protect them.

Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts have issued 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the "International LGBT Movement" or for displaying its symbols since the 2023 Supreme Court designation, comprising about 98 administrative cases and 3 criminal cases. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges; three publishing-house staff charged under article 282.2 face up to 12 years' imprisonment, and 81 people were convicted in 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols.

No separate Mordovia-specific legal instrument, enforcement record, or service provision affecting transgender visitors was present in the inventory; the national figures above are the operative baseline for a visit to Saransk or elsewhere in the republic.
tangentialFactors:
The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers. Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

Enforcement has expanded in volume alongside severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding.

The Guardian reported on 17 January 2024 that within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars: about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night. The Moscow Times reported on 23 June 2025 that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, and quoted a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation.

The Associated Press reported in December 2024 that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.
localsOnly:
For residents of Mordovia the national prohibitions are the operative rules of daily life: no legal gender recognition, no gender-marker change on official documents, no access to trans-specific healthcare, and no route to same-sex marriage. Openly LGBT+ people face societal discrimination that the UK Home Office assesses may amount to persecution, with the state able but unwilling to protect them.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note (June 2025) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.

Coercive practices against transgender residents are documented. BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 on "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping after police responded to a phone she had found.

The UK Home Office note records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024, indicating the scale of resident exposure to the legal regime over that period.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Mordovia-specific enforcement data, prosecution records, or regional directives on gender markers, healthcare access or public-order policing were present in the inventory; whether Mordovia deviates from the national position in practice is unresolved on the available sources.

The inventory contains no information on local facilities, screening practices at entry points, or the treatment of transgender travellers by Mordovia police, border officers or medical staff in Saransk; these remain unsourced rather than confirmed absent.

The count of 101 extremism-related convictions reported by Human Rights Watch is a national figure current to 30 June 2025 and is not broken down by federal subject, so the share attributable to Mordovia is unresolved.

The 2025 UK Home Office note and the 2023 statutory bans are cited at their stated dates; no later amendment to those instruments was present in the inventory.
